newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam says car import quota needs to be scrapped.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam says car import quota needs to be scrapped.

text.p: Vietnam needs to abolish quotas on the import of unassembled cars so that local joint venture manufacturers can operate to market demand, Vice Minister for Industry Nguyen Xuan Chuan said on Wednesday.

"The issue now is that quotas on cars need to be abolished so that joint ventures can develop capacity and define by themselves the number of cars to be assembled each quarter and each year according to market demand," Chuan said in remarks prepared for an industry conference.
The government currently imposes quotas for the import of unassembled vehicles, known as complete knockdown kits (CKDs).
This year's car CKD import quota is 6,000, and has to be shared among the half-dozen plants now operating with an estimated combined capacity of some 30,000 a year.
"That is the biggest thing anyone has said on this issue. I nearly fell off my chair when he said that," said one of the delegates at the conference, who declined to be named.
The government has granted licenses to 14 joint ventures to produce cars in Vietnam, a number many in the industry say has left too many scrambling for slices of a still-nascent market.
Chuan said that demand for all types of vehicle in Vietnam was expected to more than double to 80,800 units by 2005 from 39,800 last year.

However, he said that if demand continued to outstrip government projections at its current rate, the annual market could stand at 105,000 units by 2005. That would be equivalent to 77 percent of production capacity.
"...14 joint ventures is not a large number for the Vietnamese market in the next 10 years," Chuan told the conference.

He said imports of second-hand cars should be banned to allow the domestic production market to grow, and was quoted in the weekly Vietnam Investment Review as saying that 200,000 old vehicles would need to be replaced over the next 10 years.

Car manufacturers operating in Vietnam have complained that they are obliged to produce a minimum share of their components locally, starting with five percent in the first five years and at least 30 percent after 10 years.

But Chuan said that, typically, car makers were committing themselves to 7.5 percent of locally produced components in the first five years and 35 percent after the next five years. These rates could rise if the tax regime was "more encouraging."
